title: Stone Age to Chalcolithic India

cards.b: Most of India’s past has no texts. Tools, pots and bones tell the story. UPSC asks for the phases, sites and the key change from hunting to farming.

Archaeology divides prehistory by tools: Palaeolithic (Old Stone Age, to about 10,000 BCE), Mesolithic (about 10,000 to 6,000 BCE), Neolithic (from about 6,000 BCE in the north-west), Chalcolithic (copper and stone, from about 3,000 BCE), then the Iron Age. Dates vary by region. Robert Bruce Foote found the first Palaeolithic tool at Pallavaram (1863).

cards.h: Palaeolithic sites and ways of life
cards.b: Hunting and gathering; Quartzite tools: hand-axes and cleavers (Acheulian), choppers (Soan). Sites: Bhimbetka (Madhya Pradesh; rock shelters, paintings), Attirampakkam (Tamil Nadu; early tools), Hunsgi (Karnataka), Belan valley (UP), Soan valley (Punjab, Pakistan). People lived in caves and rock shelters and used fire. The climate was cold and dry in the late phase.

Microliths (tiny stone tools) set in wood or bone; bow and arrow; fishing; first domestication of the dog; beginnings of animal herding. Sites: Bagor (Rajasthan), Adamgarh (MP; early animals), Sarai Nahar Rai and Mahadaha (UP; burials, bone tools), Langhnaj (Gujarat). Rock paintings show hunt, dance and group life.

V. Gordon Childe coined the term: food production, pottery, polished stone axes, settled life. Mehrgarh (Baluchistan, c. 7000 BCE; wheat, barley, cattle; precursor of the Harappan culture). Burzahom (Kashmir; pit dwellings, dogs buried with masters), Chirand (Bihar; bone tools), Koldihwa (UP; earliest rice, c. 6000 BCE), Maski, Brahmagiri, Piklihal (Karnataka), Daojali Hading (Assam). Granaries, pottery, ash mounds in the south.

Use of copper with stone. Villages with mud houses; painted pottery; farming of wheat, barley and millet; cattle; burial of children in house floors. Sites: Ahar-Banas (Rajasthan), Kayatha (MP), Malwa (Navdatoli), Jorwe (Maharashtra; Inamgaon, a big site with burials and a granary), Prabhas and Rangpur (Gujarat). Also Ochre Coloured Pottery and the Copper Hoards (Gangetic basin). Reasons for decline: drought and lack of metal tools.

Moving to farming made villages, property and craft. Population rose. Leaders and exchange grew. It prepared the soil for the Harappan towns. The shift was slow and had many regions: in some places hunters and herders carried on beside farmers. Rock art kept the memory.

Childe’s “revolution” is now thought to be gradual. Scholars (Dorian Fuller, Jean-François Jarrige) debate whether Mehrgarh’s farming was local or brought from West Asia. Rice farming might have local roots. Evidence from Attirampakkam (2018 study dating tools to 385,000 years ago) has pushed the date for Middle Palaeolithic technology much earlier in India.

Bhimbetka (UNESCO 2003) and many rock-art sites need protection; the ASI and state bodies manage them. Archaeological methods (carbon dating, ancient DNA) help to resolve the debates. Tribal communities still use some of these skills, and traditional crops have been revived: millets (International Year of Millets, 2023).
